input:
Basis

This report presents the design of a spray dryer that dries a liquid feed to a free-flowing solid by atomising the feed into a stream of heated gas. The design throughput is 5 t per day. The removal duty is set on the key component, namely the moisture carried in with the feed: the dryer removes 97% of that moisture, and the product leaves at the residual moisture implied by the duty. Operation is continuous, with the feed supplied as a liquid that can be pumped and atomised, and the dried solid is discharged from the bottom of the drying chamber while the exhaust gas leaves together with the evaporated moisture and the finest fraction of the solid.

The basis fixes the feed in the state in which it reaches the dryer battery limit: filtered, at its supply temperature, and at a solids content within the range that the atomiser is able to handle. Heat is supplied to the drying gas upstream of the chamber; the gas acts both as the drying medium and as the transport medium for the droplets and the dried particles. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; the materials section goes on to develop the selection from the service conditions. The basis states the duty at the design throughput, and no margin is carried on throughput itself: margins in this design are held in the gas flow and the heat input, where they can actually be used in operation, rather than in the rated capacity of the chamber.

The report sizes the chamber and the principal auxiliaries, records the materials selection for the wetted parts, and registers the risks that the design does not fully close. Two risks are identified as open items: fouling and turndown. Neither of these is resolved anywhere in this report.

Sizing

The chamber is sized on the basis of the drying time of the largest droplets produced by the atomiser. A droplet needs to give up its moisture before it reaches a wall or the chamber outlet; a droplet that arrives wet will stick, while a droplet that arrives dry travels onward with the gas. The chamber diameter is determined by the gas flow and by the need to keep the spray envelope clear of the walls, and the chamber height is determined by the falling path that the largest droplets require for their drying time at the design gas temperature. The sizing therefore proceeds from the droplet rather than from the throughput: at the design throughput of 5 t per day, the feed rate fixes the liquid loading on the gas, but the chamber geometry follows the droplet trajectory and the gas residence that it requires.

The atomiser is selected to deliver the droplet size distribution that the chamber sizing assumes. Atomiser duty and chamber sizing form a matched pair: a finer spray dries more quickly and can be accommodated in a smaller chamber, at the cost of additional energy at the atomiser and a finer product that the collection system must then be able to catch. The gas system is sized together with the chamber: the heater raises the drying gas to its inlet temperature, the fans move the gas through the chamber, the collection equipment and the exhaust path against their combined resistance, and the collection system separates the dried solid from the exhaust. Cyclones take the coarse fraction and a fabric filter takes the fines; the split between them follows the particle size distribution delivered by the atomiser and the chamber, and the product stream is the sum of the two collected fractions. Exhaust treatment beyond solids collection falls outside this design. Instruments on the sized system monitor the variables that the operator is able to act on: gas inlet and outlet temperatures, chamber pressure, feed rate and product moisture, each provided with its alarm in the operating instructions.

Materials

The wetted parts of the dryer operate in three distinct services, and the selection responds to each of them. The feed system and the atomiser see the liquid feed as supplied: a process liquor that is corrosive to lesser grades under the cleaning regime applied by the plant, and the wetted surfaces must additionally withstand the wash liquors used to clean them. The chamber and the product contact surfaces see hot, moist gas on one side and a hygroscopic solid on the other; condensation forms on these surfaces whenever the unit cools down, and the condensate is effectively feed liquor in a dilute and aggressive form. The exhaust path sees the same moist gas below its dew point at the cold end, which represents the most corrosive service in the unit.

Against those services, the selection provides a grade with resistance to the feed and wash liquors, to the condensate, and to the cleaning cycle applied between campaigns, together with a surface finish on product contact parts that releases deposits and can be cleaned to the standard required by the product. Welds in wetted service are finished flush for the same reason: a crevice or a rough weld retains liquor, dries it in place, and initiates the deposit that the cleaning cycle subsequently has to remove. Non-wetted structure is specified separately, on the basis of strength and temperature alone. Elastomers and gaskets in the wetted boundary are selected for the wash liquors as well as for the feed, since a gasket that survives the process but fails in cleaning still fails in service. The exhaust duct at the cold end is treated as wetted for selection purposes, because its service is governed by condensation rather than by the dry gas temperature upstream.

Risks

Fouling is the first open item. The deposit mechanism is understood in outline: droplets that reach a surface while still wet, or particles that settle where the gas slows down, dry in place and build up a layer that alters the gas flow, insulates the surface, and eventually sheds into the product. What the design does not establish is the rate: the deposit rate on this feed, in this chamber, at the design temperatures has not been measured, and the cleaning interval that the plant would need to hold is therefore not yet known. The design responds to fouling with access, finish and cleanability, and with instrumentation that reveals a deposit forming as a drift in temperatures and pressures; it does not answer the question of how often the unit must be stopped for cleaning. That question is carried forward as an open item, and it represents the largest single uncertainty in the operating cost of the unit.

Turndown is the second open item. Spray dryer turndown is not simply a feed valve movement: at reduced feed, the atomiser produces a different droplet spectrum, the gas-to-liquid ratio increases, the outlet temperature control behaves differently, and the product moisture responds to all three effects at the same time. The removal duty of 97% is stated at the design point. The depth of turndown at which the dryer still meets that duty, with the product inside its moisture specification, has not been established by testing on this feed, and the design does not claim a figure for it. Operation below the design point is therefore an open item as well: the plant can run the dryer down, but the report cannot state how far down the product remains within specification. Both items are identified for resolution in the next design stage, through test work on the actual feed; neither is resolved in this report.
